897.title: Josephine Bakhita (c. 1869–1947)
897.hook: kidnapped in Sudan, enslaved, freed, she became a sister, patron of trafficking survivors
897.howItsDone: Catholics keep Josephine Bakhita's feast in February, and many parishes and religious orders use the day to pray for victims and survivors of human trafficking and to support groups that help them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Charles Lwanga and the Uganda martyrs, Catholic and Anglican on the same road. Your line was catholic and anglican together. Today, a woman who once had no name she could remember.

A girl in Sudan is grabbed by slave raiders. She is so terrified that, by her own later telling, she forgets the name her parents gave her. The raiders hand her another name: Bakhita. She is sold, and sold again. Owners beat her. One has her skin cut in patterns and rubbed with salt, so the scars will stay. Then an Italian consul buys her, and she ends up in Italy, caring for a family's little daughter. The family leaves the two of them for a while with some sisters in Venice. What happens in that convent ends with the law in Venice deciding who she belongs to.
screen: `A GIRL TAKEN BY RAIDERS.` → `SOLD, AND SOLD AGAIN.` → `A CONVENT IN VENICE.`

segments.voice: Start with what she kept. First, the scars. She carried them for the rest of her life, and never pretended the cruelty hadn't happened. Second, the convent. The Canossian Sisters in Venice taught her about God, and about Christ, who also suffered at the hands of others. She asked to be baptized. Third, the refusal. When her mistress came back to take her home, Bakhita said no. She wanted to stay. The mistress pushed, and the case went to the authorities in Venice. They ruled that she was free: under Italian law, nobody could own her. Fourth, the deeper freedom. She was baptized Josephine, and kept Bakhita too. Later she joined the Canossian Sisters herself, and for years she cooked, sewed, and answered the convent door in a small town. People came to that door just to talk to her. Pope Benedict XVI told her story in his letter on hope: after cruel masters, she came to know a different master, one who loved her, and that gave her hope. In John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "If therefore the son shall make you free, you shall be free indeed." Freed by a ruling. Free, she said, by being loved. The Church now names her a patron of people who survive trafficking, the slavery that still goes on.

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people who, right now, are bought and sold, or who have just gotten out: a worker who can't leave a job, a girl far from home, someone rebuilding a life. You don't need faces; let them be real anyway. If you pray, ask Josephine Bakhita to stand with them, or hold them before God in silence; if you don't, hold them in your attention and wish them freedom.
Josephine Bakhita. A woman enslaved as a girl, declared free in Venice, baptized, and made a sister, now a patron of trafficking survivors.
Your line: freed and free. The scars stayed; so did the freedom. See you tomorrow.

898.title: Katharine Drexel (1858–1955)
898.hook: an heiress who gave her fortune to schools for Black and Native Americans
898.howItsDone: Catholics in the United States keep Katharine Drexel's feast in March; the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament, Xavier University of Louisiana and Black and Native American Catholic communities mark it with Mass and service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Josephine Bakhita, declared free in Venice, and free, she said, by being loved. Your line was freed and free. Today, a banker's daughter and a question from a pope.

Rome, and a young woman from a banking family in Philadelphia kneels before Pope Leo XIII. She has come to ask a favor. Back home she has seen missions among Native American peoples that are short of priests, and she wants the Pope to send missionaries. Tradition says he answered with a question of his own: why not become a missionary yourself? It was not the answer she came for. It changed the plan. Her name is Katharine Drexel.
screen: `A BANKER'S DAUGHTER IN ROME.` → `SEND MISSIONARIES, PLEASE.` → `WHY NOT YOU?`

segments.voice: Start with the money. First, the inheritance. Her father, Francis Drexel, was a wealthy banker, and when he died, the income from his fortune passed to his daughters. Katharine's share was large. Second, the vow. Instead of marrying or living quietly on the money, she became a sister and founded a new community, the Sisters of the Blessed Sacrament. Their work was with Native Americans and Black Americans, among them children whom segregated schools often turned away. Third, the giving. Year after year she paid for schools, missions and churches, in the West and the South, in cities and on reservations. In New Orleans she and her sisters founded what became Xavier University of Louisiana. People wrote asking for help, and she answered letter after letter. Her biographers say she lived plainly herself: worn shoes, patched clothes, pencils used down to the stub. Fourth, the quiet end. After illness she spent her last years mostly in prayer, in a small room near the chapel, close to the Blessed Sacrament she had named her sisters for. In Matthew's Gospel, a rich young man asks Jesus what he must do, and Jesus tells him to sell what he has, give to the poor, and follow. The young man walks away sad, because he has many possessions. Katharine Drexel heard the same Gospel and did not walk away. The Church has since canonized her.

segments.voice: Let a child or a student come to mind whose chance to learn is fragile, and a place that helps them: a school near you, a scholarship fund, a library, a tutoring program. 899.title: Frances Cabrini (1850–1917)
899.hook: an Italian sister who served immigrants in America, patron of immigrants
899.howItsDone: Catholics in the United States keep Frances Cabrini's feast in November; parishes and Catholic charities often mark it with prayer for migrants and with service to immigrant families, and pilgrims visit her shrines in New York, Chicago and Colorado.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Katharine Drexel, who heard a pope ask why not you, and spent her inheritance on schools. Your line was she gave the fortune. Today, a sister who wanted to go east and was sent west.

New York harbor, and a ship from Italy is coming in. On deck stands a small woman in a religious habit, with a few sisters beside her. She was not supposed to be here. Since childhood she had dreamed of being a missionary in China, and she founded her own community of sisters with that in mind. Then, in Rome, she was sent the other way. And, tradition says, she is afraid of water. Her name is Frances Xavier Cabrini.
screen: `A SHIP INTO NEW YORK.` → `A DREAM OF CHINA.` → `SENT THE OTHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Start with the order. First, the redirect. Her community was the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart, and she went to Rome to ask permission to take them to China. Tradition says Pope Leo XIII told her: not to the East, but to the West. Italian families were arriving in American cities, often poor, with few priests or sisters who spoke their language. Second, the arrival. When they landed, tradition says the house they'd been promised wasn't ready, and the archbishop suggested they might go back to Italy. She stayed. Third, the work and the crossings. She and her sisters ran classes for immigrant children, opened orphanages, and started hospitals, beginning in New York and spreading to other cities and countries. They went into tenements and jails, wherever Italian families were struggling. Tradition says she had nearly drowned as a child, yet she crossed the ocean again and again, because the work kept calling. Fourth, the citizen. She became an American citizen herself. She died in Chicago, and the Church later canonized her and named her a patron of immigrants. In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus speaks of the final judgment: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." For Cabrini, the stranger was the family off the boat, the child in a crowded room, the sick person far from home. That's why people call her the immigrants' saint: she spent her life on immigrants, and became one herself.

segments.voice: Think of someone who came from somewhere else: a neighbor, a coworker, the person who cleans your building, someone in your own family tree. Picture their first weeks, the forms, the language, not knowing where anything is, and let one concrete help come to mind: a ride, a translation, a meal, a patient conversation. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, hold them in your attention.

900.title: Story of a Soul (1898)
900.hook: Thérèse's memoir is published and goes around the world
900.howItsDone: Some Catholics read Story of a Soul on retreat or around Thérèse's feast in October, and parishes and prayer groups sometimes read it together a chapter at a time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Frances Cabrini, sent west instead of east, an immigrant serving immigrants. Your line was the immigrants' saint. Today, a book nobody planned to sell.

A notebook, a pen, and a young nun in a Carmelite convent in Lisieux, in France. Her older sister, who is also her prioress, has asked her to write down memories of their childhood. So Thérèse writes: her family, her mother's death, her tears, her first communion, the convent. Later, already sick, she is asked to write more, and she keeps going in a garden chair, then in bed. She began it for her sisters, not for strangers; only near the end does she speak of the pages being printed. After she dies, the convent prints them: Story of a Soul.
screen: `A NOTEBOOK IN LISIEUX.` → `WRITTEN FOR HER SISTERS.` → `PRINTED AFTER SHE DIES.`

segments.voice: Follow the book. First, the writing. Thérèse wrote in pieces, under obedience, in ordinary notebooks. She wasn't composing a classic; she was answering her sisters. Second, the editing. Her sister Pauline, Mother Agnes, prepared the pages for print and smoothed them in places. Much later, the original notebooks were published as Thérèse wrote them, so readers could see her own words. Third, the spreading. Carmelite convents would send a short account of a sister's life to other houses after her death. This one was different. It was copied, reprinted, translated, passed from hand to hand. Tradition says letters came back to Lisieux from readers: soldiers, mothers, missionaries, people in prison. Fourth, the little way. What readers found was not a story of great deeds but a way: do small things with love, trust God like a child, and don't wait to become impressive first. In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says: "unless you be converted, and become as little children, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven." Thérèse took that line seriously. The Church later canonized her and named her a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for the whole Church. Much of what she taught reached readers through one little book, written for her sisters.
screen: `NOTEBOOKS, UNDER OBEDIENCE.` · `A SISTER'S EDITING.` · `PASSED HAND TO HAND.` · `THE LITTLE WAY.` · then, large: `BECOME AS LITTLE CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: If you have the book, open it anywhere and read one page slowly; if not, take today's line, become as little children. Then go through one small task from today in your mind, a dish, a message, a chore you've been avoiding, slowly, done with care. If you pray, offer it to God; if not, notice how small and how real it is.
Little way. Thérèse's idea that small things done with love, and trusting God like a child, matter more than impressive deeds: the heart of Story of a Soul.
Your line: a little book. Notebooks for her sisters, read far beyond them. Nine hundred days now.

901.title: Communion for children (1905–1910)
901.hook: Pius X encourages frequent communion and first communion around age seven
901.howItsDone: In the Latin Church, Catholic children usually prepare for first communion at around seven or eight, often in a parish class, after a first confession; adults who are in a state of grace may receive communion at any Mass, even daily.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Story of a Soul and Thérèse's little way, notebooks for her sisters that traveled the world. Your line was a little book. Today, a pope who opened the altar rail to children.

A white dress, or a small suit and tie. A row of children walking up the aisle, hands folded, trying not to giggle. Grandparents with cameras in the pews. In a Catholic parish, first communion is a big day, and it comes when a child is still small. That timing has a history. Before it changed, children were often kept waiting longer, and adults who did go to communion might go only rarely, out of a sense that they were never worthy enough. A pope named Pius X set out to change both habits.
screen: `A ROW OF CHILDREN IN THE AISLE.` → `A DAY THAT USED TO COME LATER.` → `A POPE CHANGES THE HABIT.`

segments.voice: Two documents did the work. First, the hesitation. A strict mood in parts of the Church had taught people to keep their distance from the altar, as if communion were a prize for the nearly perfect. Second, the invitation to adults. A decree under Pius X said communion could be received often, even daily, by anyone in a state of grace who comes with a right intention. Communion was described not as a reward for the holy but as help for the weak. Come often. Third, the children. A second decree, known by its opening Latin words, Quam singulari, took up the age of first communion. It said the age of discretion is when a child begins to reason, about the seventh year, more or less, and that children should not be kept waiting long past it. A child didn't need to understand everything a theologian knows. They needed to know, in their own way, that this bread is not ordinary bread, and to want it. Fourth, the root. The decrees leaned on Jesus's words in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "Except you eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you." If the bread is life, the reasoning went, why make the hungry wait? The small children walking up the aisle today follow a path opened by two documents from one pope.
screen: `KEEPING A DISTANCE.` · `HELP FOR THE WEAK, NOT A PRIZE.` · `THE AGE OF DISCRETION.` · `BREAD THAT IS LIFE.` · then, large: `COME OFTEN.`

segments.voice: Think back to your first communion, if you made one: the clothes, the church, who was there. If you didn't, remember a first time at any table that mattered, a meal where you were welcomed, and notice who brought you there. If you pray, thank God for that person by name; if not, hold them with gratitude.
Quam singulari. The decree under Pius X that said children should make their first communion once they reach the age of discretion, about seven years old.

902.title: Charles de Foucauld (1858–1916)
902.hook: a soldier turned hermit among the Tuareg, the universal brother, canonized a saint
902.howItsDone: Catholics keep Charles de Foucauld's memory on 1 December; communities inspired by him, such as the Little Brothers and Little Sisters of Jesus, live simply in small groups among poor neighbors and keep long times of silent prayer before the Eucharist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Quam singulari, and a pope who called communion help for the weak. Your line was come often. Today, a man who went a very long way to be a neighbor.

A young French cavalry officer, rich, bored, famous among his friends for parties and expensive food. He has lost his faith and doesn't miss it. He leaves the army and travels through Morocco in disguise to map it, and the trip makes his name as an explorer. But something else follows him home: the memory of Muslims stopping to pray, again and again, every day. Back in Paris, he starts slipping into churches and repeating a strange little prayer: if you exist, let me know you. His name is Charles de Foucauld.
screen: `AN OFFICER WHO LOVES PARTIES.` → `MOROCCO, IN DISGUISE.` → `IF YOU EXIST, LET ME KNOW YOU.`

segments.voice: First, the confession. In a Paris church, he went to a priest, Abbé Huvelin, to talk about faith. The priest told him to kneel and confess, then sent him to communion. Charles later wrote that as soon as he believed there was a God, he knew he could only live for him. Second, Nazareth. He tried the strict life of a Trappist monastery, then went to Nazareth and worked as a handyman for a convent of sisters, living the hidden years of Jesus, the carpenter's years nobody wrote down. Third, the desert. Ordained a priest, he went to the Sahara in French Algeria. At Beni Abbès he called his little house the fraternity. At last he settled at Tamanrasset, among the Tuareg people. He didn't preach sermons at them. He visited, nursed, shared tea, and spent years writing a Tuareg dictionary and collecting their poems. He wanted to be the universal brother: brother to Christians, Muslims, and anyone who knocked. Fourth, the door. During the upheavals of the war, raiders came to his house, and he was killed at his own door. He died alone, with no followers. In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus tells his followers: "one is your master; and all you are brethren." Charles took the second half as literally as the first. Groups of priests, sisters and laypeople now follow his way, and the Church has canonized him.

segments.voice: Hold in mind one person who sits a little outside your circle: someone who eats lunch alone, a neighbor you've never spoken to, someone whose language or faith differs from yours. Don't plan a speech; just keep them in your attention as a brother or a sister, and picture the small visit Charles might have made, a cup of tea, a question. If you pray, pray for them by name.

903.title: Fatima, 1917
903.hook: three shepherd children and a call to prayer and penance
903.howItsDone: Catholics keep Our Lady of Fatima on 13 May; pilgrims go to the shrine at Fatima, and in parishes people pray the rosary together, often adding a prayer for peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Charles de Foucauld, the soldier who became a universal brother among the Tuareg. Your line was brother to everyone. Today, shepherd children, and a jail cell.

A town official in Portugal loads some children into his carriage. They are shepherds from the hamlet of Aljustrel, near Fatima: Lucia and her cousins Francisco and Jacinta. For months they have said that a lady from heaven appears to them on the thirteenth of each month, and crowds now follow them to the field. The official is not a believer, and his government is suspicious of the Church. He wants the crowds gone and the children's secret out. Instead of taking them to the field, he takes them to his town and locks them up.
screen: `A CARRIAGE, A TOWN OFFICIAL.` → `CROWDS IN A FIELD.` → `CHILDREN LOCKED UP.`

segments.voice: Stay with those few days. First, the message. The children said the lady asked them to pray the rosary every day for peace and the end of the war, and to do penance, small sacrifices offered for others. Europe was at war, and Portuguese soldiers were in it. Second, the pressure. In Lucia's later memoirs, the official questioned them, and when they refused to tell what the lady had confided, he threatened them with death. They were frightened. They still wouldn't tell. Third, the cell. Lucia recalled that they were put in a room with the town's prisoners. Jacinta was crying for her mother. Then the children knelt and began the rosary, and some of the prisoners knelt and prayed with them: grown men in a jail, following children through the Hail Mary. Fourth, the outcome. The children were sent home, and they said the lady came again a few days later, in a different spot. In the end the Church judged the appearances worthy of belief; Catholics are free to accept them or not, since the Church calls such events private revelations. At the center is a prayer older than Fatima, the angel's words in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." This week ran through a freed slave, an heiress, an immigrant, a little book, children at the altar, a desert brother, and now children praying in a jail.
screen: `THE ROSARY, FOR PEACE.` · `THREATENED, AND SILENT.` · `PRISONERS KNEEL WITH CHILDREN.` · `WORTHY OF BELIEF, NOT REQUIRED.` · then, large: `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.`

segments.voice: A whole rosary won't fit here, so take a small piece of it. Bring to mind one place at war right now; if you pray, say the Hail Mary slowly, once or a few times, for the people there, on beads or on your fingers. If you don't, hold that place in silence and wish its people safety and an end to the fighting.
Fatima. A village in Portugal where, the children said, a lady asked for the rosary, penance, and prayer for peace.
